item.title: Tower for Humanity Twin Towers near completion at Micronesia Mall

item.content:encoded:
The Tower for Humanity’s latest project is nearing completion at the Micronesia Mall, where brothers Landon and Brandon Aydlett are constructing a 25-foot replica of the World Trade Center Twin Towers using more than 100,000 toy timber logs.

The project marks the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks and is intended to remember those who lost their lives that day and in the years that followed. The towers are being constructed piece by piece in the mall’s Center Court. The project is expected to remain on display through Sept. 20, with disassembly scheduled for Sept. 21. For Aydlett Brothers, the project is also part of a larger effort to use their tower builds to bring attention to community needs.

Be Heartfelt provides weekend meal packs to children experiencing food insecurity. According to the organization, the program currently serves more than 350 children on Guam each week, with services extending to children in need in Saipan and Palau.

The Tower for Humanity partnership with Be Heartfelt will continue through the fourth annual Cans for Humanity Guam Competition.

The competition will follow an island-wide canned food drive throughout September and early October.

The Tower for Humanity team will also partner with Guam’s Offices of Homeland Security and Civil Defense for a National Preparedness Month Outreach Fair on September 19.

The fair will take place from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. at Micronesia Mall.

Local and federal agencies involved in emergency management, preparedness, and disaster response will provide information about disaster awareness and preparation.

For the Aydlett brothers, the project represents more than the construction of a large toy timber structure. It has become a way to connect community members with organizations working on issues in the community.

item.title: GEDA hosts Hafa Adai Festival in Japan, showcases Guam products
item.description: The Guam Economic Development Authority hosted its inaugural Håfa Adai Guam Festival in Japan, showcasing products from seven local companies to the Japan market. GEDA says thousands attended the festival in Shizuoka, between Tokyo and Nagoya.
item.content:encoded:
The Guam Economic Development Authority hosted its inaugural Håfa Adai Guam Festival in Japan, showcasing products from seven local companies to the Japan market.

GEDA says thousands attended the festival in Shizuoka, between Tokyo and Nagoya.

Gov. Lou Leon Guerrero said the festival is a celebration of the longstanding ties between Japan and Guam. The goal is to allow Guam businesses to have a stronger direct consumer presence in Japan.

Participating companies included Asiga, Denanche Guam, Everything Guam, Local Jerk Guam, Green Turtle Coffee, Kingfisher’s Noni, and The Coconut Tree Company.

item.content:encoded:
Del. Kimberlyn King‑Hinds on Sept. 7 announced that Saipan native Sgt. Nathan Jacob F. Nogis of the U.S. Army’s 25th Infantry Division has been awarded the Soldier’s Medal, the military’s highest honor for heroism outside of combat, for rescuing two people from dangerous waters in Pearl Harbor.

The award recognizes Nogis’ actions on Oct. 26, 2024, when he responded to a desperate call for help involving two individuals stranded in the Pearl Harbor Ship Channel. With Harbor Patrol unable to immediately reach the scene, Nogis relied on his survival training, improvisation, and determination to act.

According to King‑Hinds, Nogis secured the only available flotation device — a small, youth‑sized boogie board — and entered the water despite strong currents, waves exceeding three feet, and hazardous conditions. For more than four hours and across roughly two miles, he fought exhaustion and the current to reach the victims.

After locating the two individuals, Nogis continued swimming against the current to bring them toward safety, ultimately rescuing both and helping ensure they survived.

King‑Hinds said Nogis’ willingness to risk his own life to save others reflects “the courage, selflessness, and highest traditions of military service,” adding that his actions make the CNMI proud.

“I am proud to congratulate Sergeant Nathan Jacob F. Nogis on being awarded the Soldier’s Medal, recognizing his extraordinary heroism and selfless service,” she said. “Thank you, Sgt. Nogis, for your service, your courage, and your commitment to saving others.”

The Soldier’s Medal is awarded for acts of heroism involving personal hazard or danger and voluntary risk of life under conditions not involving conflict with an armed enemy.

item.title: New report shows the economic toll of ICE raids
item.description: A new study shows that the widespread fear and isolation caused by the immigration crackdowns that began in early 2025 had a significant economic toll on Chicago commerce, draining over $1.26 billion from local businesses. item.content:encoded:
A new study shows that the widespread fear and isolation caused by the immigration crackdowns that began in early 2025 had a significant economic toll on Chicago commerce, draining over $1.26 billion from local businesses.

The report , published by the University of Illinois Chicago, used anonymous cellphone GPS data to track movement between immigrant and non-immigrant neighborhoods throughout Chicago's Cook County. Researchers found that the routine back-and-forth between these areas collapsed almost immediately after President Donald Trump took office on Jan. 20, 2025, amid rampant rumors and the subsequent sweeps that Chicago would be targeted for immediate Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) raids.

Professor Matt Wilson, a co-author of the study, noted how strongly the economic ripples were felt outside of immigrant communities in the area. The report estimates that decreased consumer mobility cost retail shops and restaurants in non-immigrant neighborhoods roughly $1.26 billion, while costing the state of Illinois an estimated $107 million in lost tax revenue.

"We see a 9% drop in retail and a 10% drop in restaurant visits, and it persisted for about a year," Wilson told NPR. "And it's not that it recovered after a year. People's behavior systematically changed after January 20, 2025." He says the city has yet to recover.

For small businesses, a sustained 10% drop in foot traffic business over the course of a year can be a serious financial hit. The new study challenges assumptions about immigrant community isolation, Wilson added. "I think a lot of people treat Latino and some immigrant communities as if they're insular and isolated," Wilson said. "But it's really that these communities are much more integrated into the broader economy, and they are making trips to faraway places in the county, routinely."

The intense fear that triggered these behavior shifts was palpable in the days surrounding the 2025 inauguration.

"I have to go grocery shopping, but I haven't. What if ICE is there?" a Chicago waitress named Caridad told NPR at the time, requesting that her last name be withheld, for fear of being targeted. "People are more than afraid, they're panicking."

Since then, the administration's immigration crackdowns have resulted in hundreds of thousands of arrests nationwide. Today, the immigration detention population sits at a record high of approximately 65,000 people .

The White House defended the aggressive enforcement strategy. In a statement to NPR, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said, "Removing these criminals from the streets makes communities safer for business owners and customers. Nearly 70% of ICE arrests are of illegal aliens charged or convicted of a crime in the U.S."

However, ICE's own agency statistics show that roughly 70% of those currently detained have no criminal convictions.

The new report is part of a growing body of research confirming that large-scale immigration enforcement operations send severe economic shockwaves through broader local economies. A Brookings Institution report estimates estimates a roughly 1.7 percentage point decline in aggregate consumer spending in high-enforcement states

In Minneapolis, the city estimates total economic damage from ICE enforcement sweeps there at nearly $700 million, with small businesses in the city losing more than $81 million in revenue in January alone.

item.title: Kenya's foreign trader crackdown sparks fear among migrant communities
item.description: NAIROBI, Kenya — In Kibera, one of Nairobi's largest informal settlements, it's another busy morning. People rush to work, hailing matatus along the roadside as vendors set up for the day. But for foreign nationals who run small businesses here, it's far from business as usual.
item.content:encoded:
NAIROBI, Kenya — In Kibera, one of Nairobi's largest informal settlements, it's another busy morning. People rush to work, hailing matatus along the roadside as vendors set up for the day.

But for foreign nationals who run small businesses here, it's far from business as usual.

Last week, President William Ruto ordered authorities to shut down small-scale businesses operated by foreign traders, saying such work should be left to Kenyans.

The president gave them until this week to comply, prompting fear among migrant communities.

At a matatu terminal in Nairobi, James Mogaka is already seeing the impact. He manages a hub for the country's ubiquitous minibus taxis and says many of the vehicles are owned or operated by foreign nationals.

"Today they have not come. Their vehicles are not here," he says.

Mogaka says one of his drivers is too scared to come to work and is worried about his wife, a Burundian national who runs a fruit business.

"The guy is even afraid that people might come to chase away the wife," he says. "I really don't know where we are heading."

The government announcement has left migrant communities anxious about the potential impact on their livelihoods and safety.

It also comes against a backdrop of rising tensions over migration and foreign-owned businesses in parts of Africa — from restrictions on non-citizens running certain businesses in Tanzania to a resurgence of xenophobic violence in South Africa.

The unease is palpable in Kenya, where many people affected by the directive were reluctant to speak to us on the record.

In Nairobi's central business district, the directive is drawing a mixed reaction.

Local trader Robert Kiberenge opposes the move. "The president is just trying to divert our attention from more pressing issues. We have no problem with foreigners doing small businesses in Kenya."

But there is also support for the president's move. Graduate Kiprono Kutuny is among those who back it.

"I concur with him. The government needs to protect the traders and small business people, but you find that these people who come from different foreign countries have taken these businesses and they are doing it in a cheap labor."

Kenya is East Africa's economic hub and is known for its relative political stability. The United Nations estimates put the number of international migrants living in Kenya at about 993,000 in 2024.

The government says the policy is intended to protect Kenyan traders in a crowded small-business sector, where competition from foreign nationals has become an increasingly contentious issue.

But economist Edward Kusewa says the President Ruto's directive is the wrong move. "I think it's very uncalled for."

Kusewa says the policy could undermine the principles of the African Continental Free Trade Area , which aims to ease the movement of goods and people across borders.

"These people contribute a lot to the economy," Kusewa says." They pay taxes directly and I think this is going to have an impact on the Kenyan economy."

Ruto faces voters next year, with the debate over who gets to operate small businesses unfolding against a backdrop of economic pressures and concerns over jobs and livelihoods.

As the government tries to reassure those affected, foreign nationals — many from neighbouring countries including Burundi and the Democratic Republic of Congo — have been turning to their embassies for help securing documents to return home.

On Tuesday, in an effort to ease concerns, the government gave undocumented East African nationals 90 days to obtain or update the documents required to stay and do business in Kenya.

But for many, the fear of what comes next has already taken hold.

item.title: Smithsonian chief Lonnie G. Bunch III resigns
item.description: Updated September 9, 2026 at 10:18 AM ChST Lonnie G. Bunch III, secretary of the Smithsonian Institution, is stepping down from his post at the end of the year.
item.content:encoded:
Updated September 9, 2026 at 10:18 AM ChST

Lonnie G. Bunch III, secretary of the Smithsonian Institution, is stepping down from his post at the end of the year.

"It is with very mixed emotions and heartfelt gratitude that I announce my retirement," Bunch wrote in a statement. "I leave with pride and sadness, gratitude and joy, and with enormous confidence in the people who will carry this remarkable institution forward."

The Smithsonian Institution — which includes dozens of museums, libraries, research centers, and the National Zoo — has been a frequent target of criticism by President Trump. In August 2025, Trump called for a "comprehensive internal review" of eight Smithsonian museums, and directed them to "celebrate American exceptionalism." In July 2026, the Trump administration issued a report accusing the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History of "extreme political activism."

Bunch defended the museum internally. "At the Smithsonian, our work is driven by scholarship, accuracy and an uncompromising commitment to tell the fullness of America's story," he wrote in an email to his staff in July, obtained by NPR.

In an interview with NPR on Tuesday , 73-year-old Bunch said he knew it was time because, in his words, "I'm old as dirt."

"The reality as that after 38 years, I've been able to accomplish so much, I've learned so much, I've built such great relationships, and now I want to make sure that I have time to write, to think, and really to bore my grandkids to death. And now's the moment to do it."

He said that the president's criticism of the Smithsonian wasn't part of his decision. But, he said, the independence of the institution is essential.

"It's important to realize that the Smithsonian celebrates and loves America," he said. "The work we do explains the complexity of America."

Bunch, the 14th secretary of the Smithsonian, has had a long career in museums, including four decades at the Smithsonian. In 2005, he became the founding director of the Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History and Culture. There, he oversaw the conception and construction of the museum's building on the National Mall, which opened in September 2016 .

In 2019, Bunch was named secretary of the Smithsonian, becoming the first historian and the first African American to hold the position. There he pushed forward plans for two museums — the Smithsonian American Women's History Museum and the National Museum of the American Latino, and he has been leading the institution's fundraising efforts.

The institution's Board of Regents have yet to name an acting chief, but have announced the beginning of a national search for a new secretary.

item.title: How Caroline Rose threw out the rulebook on their latest album
item.description: You cannot put Caroline Rose into a box. Even Caroline Rose can't put Caroline Rose into a box. Rose has always pushed against expectations, whether it's an industry that exploits artists, which led them to start their own independent record label, or their own ideas about what a "serious artist" is supposed to look and sound like.
item.content:encoded:
You cannot put Caroline Rose into a box. Even Caroline Rose can't put Caroline Rose into a box.

Rose has always pushed against expectations, whether it's an industry that exploits artists, which led them to start their own independent record label, or their own ideas about what a "serious artist" is supposed to look and sound like.

Today, Rose joins me to talk about their new album, Gentling the Horse at the Walt Whitman Mall , out Oct. 23. They talk about learning to trust their instincts as a songwriter and performer, making room for fun and building a career outside the traditional music industry.

Rose also performs live, beginning with a song they've been playing for nearly a decade but only recently recorded for the new album.

This episode of World Cafe was produced and edited by Kimberly Junod. Our digital producer is Miguel Perez. World Cafe 's engineer is Chris Williams. Our programming and booking coordinator is Chelsea Johnson and our line producer is Will Loftus.
